Son of Hugh Giffard of Boyton and Sybil de Cormeilles, he rose with his elder brother Walter, Archbishop of York. He became canon and archdeacon of Wells, then Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1266 and Chancellor of England later that year. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a bishop who ruled his diocese nearly thirty-four years.

Elected by the monks of Worcester, he received the temporalities in June 1268. He was consecrated at Canterbury that September and enthroned at Christmas. During his chancellorship a parliament at Marlborough passed useful laws restraining abuses of distress, regulating tenure, and improving civil and criminal procedure. As bishop he finished and fortified Hartlebury Castle, ever since the bishops' principal palace, and wrestled with long feuds with the cathedral monks and Malvern Priory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gunning-s-bed:
Baltimore physician Gunning S. Bedford, born in 1806 and named for his uncle, a framer of the American Constitution, became a leading teacher of obstetrics in the United States. After Mount St. Mary's College and a medical degree from Rutgers, plus two years of study abroad, he held chairs at Charleston at twenty-six and then at Albany.

Moving to New York in 1836, he founded the University Medical College four years later. Beside it he opened the country's first obstetrical clinic for women too poor to pay a doctor, a boon for the poor and for medicine alike. He taught until illness stopped him in 1862. His Diseases of Women and Practice of Obstetrics ran through many editions in French and German as American textbooks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hartford:
Connecticut's Diocese of Hartford, erected by Gregory XVI in September 1843, first covered Connecticut and Rhode Island, with its bishop living at Providence until a new see rose there in 1872. Now matching Connecticut alone, it holds 375,000 Catholics, a third of the state's people, across about five thousand square miles.

Colonial Catholics were few and often priestless, from Irish soldiers of the Pequot war to 400 Acadians scattered in 1756 who lost the faith without clergy. Bernard O'Cavanaugh became the first resident priest in 1828, and at the diocese's birth only three priests served Connecticut. William Tyler, its first bishop, lived in a shanty at Providence, begged priests from Dublin, and died of consumption in 1849 after five years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-bard:
Henry Bard, a soldier and diplomat born in 1604, travelled through France, Italy, Turkey, Palestine, and Egypt before taking a fellowship at King's College, Cambridge. A favourite of Charles I, he took up arms in the Civil War and was wounded and lost an arm at Cheriton Down. He later burned Camden House rather than surrender it to Parliament. He governed Worcester, scaled the ramparts at Naseby, and became Baron Bard and Viscount Bellamont in Ireland in 1646.

While travelling to Ireland, Bard was captured and freed on promising to go overseas. The court at The Hague became his refuge. Arrested in 1649 on a murder charge that came to nothing, he was sent by Charles II in 1656 as ambassador to the Shah of Persia. He sought funds for recovering the throne. The mission failed, since Persia owed England aid given at Ormuz. Bard died in a windstorm in Arabia about 1660.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-bedford:
Henry Bedford, born in London in 1816, entered Cambridge intending to become an Anglican clergyman and became a popular High Church writer and preacher. A strongly Tractarian sermon set him against the Bishop of London, and he converted to Catholicism in 1851. A defect in his right hand barred him canonically from ordination, so he turned instead to education, joining the staff of All Hallows Missionary College near Dublin in 1852.

At All Hallows, Bedford spent half a century as professor of natural science, treasurer, and director, while writing constantly for Catholic periodicals and lecturing on Catholic subjects. His essays ranged across travel, archaeology, art, science, music, and English literature, appearing chiefly in The Month, The Irish Monthly, and The Irish Ecclesiastical Record. His Vacation Rambles, issued in a series through the 1870s, gathered some of the best of that periodical work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-herf:
Henry of Herford, a Dominican friar and chronicler who died at Minden on 9 October 1370, was a native of Herford in Westphalia and professed in the Dominican friary at Minden. He compiled his chronicle Liber de Rebus Memorabilioribus there, summarizing older historians from Eusebius down to writers of his own age. It continues to the coronation of Emperor Charles IV in 1355. It became a chief source of historical knowledge for the fourteenth century and was printed under Potthast's editorship at Göttingen in 1859.

Henry also composed the Catena Aurea, a summary of theology in ten parts, and a still unpublished treatise on the conception of the glorious Virgin. The entry thus preserves a monastic compiler whose value lay less in originality than in gathering and ordering the historical knowledge available to his century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-ward:
Hugh Ward, in Irish Aedh Buidh Mac-an-Bhaird, was an Irish hagiographer, born in Donegal about 1590 and dead in 1635. His father Geoffrey, chief of Lettermacward, led the Tirconnell branch of the Mac-an-Bhaird, who from remote times cultivated literature and served as chief historians to the O'Donnells. In 1607 Ward left Ireland for Spain and entered Salamanca University.

There Luke Wadding met him and guided him into the Franciscans in 1616. After degrees and ordination he lectured on philosophy at Paris and became Louvain's St. Anthony's College professor of divinity, elected its rector in 1626. Wadding praised his intellect and Irish learning, and Ponce ranked his scholastic lectures second to none. Ward's chief passion, though, was Irish saints' lives and ancient records, a publishing plan he pioneered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humphrey-beri:
Humphrey Berisford was an English confessor of about 1588. He is known only from a seventeenth-century manuscript compiled by Father Christopher Grene, now at the English College in Rome and partly printed in Foley's Records. The account calls him a Derbyshire gentleman whose father, an esquire, was Protestant.

Berisford studied at Douay about two years. Returning home, his father set him to a lawsuit, and an opponent, fearing defeat, accused him before the judge as a recusant. Examined, he constantly professed his faith. The judge offered favour to his suit and liberty if he would only promise to attend the established church, which he utterly refused. He was therefore imprisoned, where he remained seven years, the account's blank plausibly filled, and died a prisoner at Derby Gaol.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-echar:
Jacques Echard, a Dominican historian, was born at Rouen on 22 September 1644 and died at Paris on 15 March 1724. As the son of a wealthy royal official, he got a thorough grounding in classical and secular learning. He joined the Dominican order at Paris and stood out for hard study, and when Jacques Quétif died in 1698, Echard picked up his unfinished project.

Quétif had mapped out a literary history of the Dominican order and had pulled together close to a fourth of its material; Echard was charged with finishing the work. After long labor and research in most of Europe's libraries, the history came out in 1721, filling two quarto volumes under the title Scriptores ordinis praedicatorum. Each writer's sketch sets out a list of works, with dates and edition details, and Echard likewise lists unpublished, spurious, and doubtful works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-ambrose:
James Ambrose Dominic Aylward, theologian and poet, was born at Leeds on 4 April 1813 and died at Hinckley in England on 5 October 1872. He was schooled at Hinckley's Dominican priory. He joined the Dominican order and took priestly orders in 1836. He rose to provincial in 1850, to first prior of Woodchester in 1854, and to provincial once more in 1866. He wrote several devout manuals for his community.

His Novena for the Holy Season of Advent, drawn from missal and breviary prophecies and anthems, came out at Derby in 1849. In 1867 he re-edited a life of St Catherine of Siena, rendered from Italian by John Fen in 1609. That same year he issued an English version of Chocarne's Inner Life of Lacordaire. Essays dealing with mystical elements in religion, and with spiritism old and modern, appeared after his death under Cardinal Manning's editorship in 1874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Blanchard, born Duchesne at Tourteron in 1731 and dead in 1797, was a French Jesuit educator who wrote under a changed name. He joined the Society in 1746, taught at Metz, Verdun, and Pont-à-Mousson, and left the order in 1762, settling near Namur to study teaching.

Blanchard's books on fables and morals led to his chief work, a guide to Christian education of both sexes, printed after his death in 1803. Borrowing Rousseau's Emile yet judging it keenly, he split schooling into body, morals, and girls' training, stressing health and hygiene. Though little in it was new, teachers prized its sound picks and plain advice.

Père Girard, born Jean-Baptiste Girard at Fribourg in 1765 and dead there in 1850, was a Swiss Franciscan who remade his canton's schools. He entered the order at sixteen, taught in its colleges, studied at Würzburg, and returned to Fribourg in 1789 for mission and teaching work.

As director of Fribourg's schools from 1807 to 1823, Girard made schooling compulsory, set up sound administration and textbooks, and used pupil monitors while fighting rote memory drill. Every subject, he held, should serve the child's whole growth. His reforms drew bitter foes wedded to old routine, yet they crowned his life's work and outlasted the quarrels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-louis-bo:
Jean-Louis Bonnard, a French missionary and martyr born in 1824 at Saint-Christôt-en-Jarret and beheaded in 1852, studied at Saint-Jodard and the Lyons seminary before finishing at Paris's foreign missions seminary. Ordained at Nantes, he sailed for western Tonkin and arrived in May 1850.

Put in charge of two parishes in 1851, Bonnard was seized on 21 March 1852 and jailed. Sentence of death, once confirmed by the king, was carried out at once on 30 April. His body, cast into a river, was recovered by Christians and sent to the foreign missions seminary. The Church has declared him Venerable, a witness honoured for dying on mission ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-nicolas-:
Jean-Nicolas Beauregard, a French Jesuit preacher born at Metz in 1733 and dead in Germany in 1804, joined the Society at Nancy in 1749. After teaching classics and rhetoric for six years at Nancy, Verdun, Strasbourg, and Pont-à-Mousson, he turned to preaching in 1767, the work of his life.

Beauregard won fame in smaller French towns, then still greater success in Paris. His Lent sermons before the court in 1789 were said to foretell the evils about to engulf France. Fleeing revolution in 1794, he lived in London, Maastricht, and Cologne, ending his days at a princess's castle, his sermons mostly still in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-picard:
Jean Picard, a French astronomer born at La Flèche in 1620 and dead in Paris in 1682. A priest and prior of Rillé, he studied under Gassendi and watched the 1645 solar eclipse with him. In 1655 he succeeded his master as astronomy professor at the Collège de France.

Picard's chief feat was measuring a meridian arc from Sourdon to Malvoisine in 1669 and 1670, fixing a degree at 57,060 toises, only fourteen too small. He fitted telescopes and micrometers to instruments from 1667, read angles to a quarter minute, and tied his standard rod to a seconds pendulum so it could be remade. Newton used his figures to revise his own reckoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bromyard:
John Bromyard was a Dominican theologian and a leading opponent of John Wyclif. Named for his birthplace in Herefordshire, he entered the Dominican order, distinguished himself at Oxford in theology and jurisprudence, and labored in the theology faculty at Cambridge. He died about 1390.

His name does not appear in the acts of the London Synod of 1382, where Archbishop Courtenay condemned Wyclif's doctrines as heretical. Yet all agree he led in drafting the decree of condemnation. His Summa for Preachers, prized enough to run through many editions, was excerpted into pamphlets widely circulated among the people. His Opus Trivium arranged topics from theology and civil and canon law for preachers' convenience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gerard:
John Gerard was an English Jesuit whose autobiography is a classic record of the underground priesthood under Elizabeth. Born in 1564, second son of Sir Thomas Gerard of Bryn, he left home at thirteen for Douai. He studied at Oxford and the Jesuit college at Paris. After two years in the Marshalsea prison he reached Rome in 1586 and entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1588.

Sent back to England within a year, he landed alone on the Norfolk coast amid the Armada panic. Feeling against Catholics then ran so high that priests were being butchered in London. An accomplished horseman and sportsman, he traveled disguised as huntsman or lost rider. He won the friendship of Catholic families, made frequent conversions, gave retreats, and sent youths and nuns to the Continent. A Protestant scholar called the extent of his influence nothing less than marvelous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lingard:
John Lingard was an English priest and historian whose History of England set a new standard for Catholic scholarship. Born at Winchester in 1771 to Lincolnshire yeomen driven by poverty and persecution, he entered Douai in 1782. He led his class at nearly every examination and escaped the Revolution to England, where he helped care for Douai refugees at Tudhoe, Pontop, and Crook Hall.

Teaching philosophy and church history, he found his true bent in the subject. He produced a History of the Anglo-Saxon Church from fireside lectures, then a school epitome that grew into his great History of England. The entry stresses the stubborn longing for England's conversion inherited from two centuries of oppression. It also stresses the patient scholarship with which Lingard, working far from London's libraries, answered Protestant histories on their own ground before his death at Hornby in 1851.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-oxenford:
John Oxenford was an English dramatist, critic, and translator whose essay introduced Schopenhauer to England. Born in London in 1812, mostly self-educated under the erratic scholar S. T. Friend, he was articled to a solicitor in 1837, wrote on commerce and finance, and remained always a devourer of books in German, Italian, French, and Spanish.

His translations of Fischer on Bacon, Goethe's autobiography, and Eckermann's Conversations with Goethe became near English classics in Bohn's series, alongside Moliere's Tartuffe and parts of Boiardo and Calderon. But drama was his chief interest: at least sixty-eight plays from 1835 to his death, librettos, and twenty years as dramatic critic of the Times. His Westminster Review essay of April 1853 is said to have founded Schopenhauer's fame in England and abroad.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-rose-gre:
John Rose Greene Hassard was an American editor and critic, first editor of the Catholic World. Born in New York in 1836 to Episcopalian parents, his mother a granddaughter of Commodore Nicholson, he became a Catholic at fifteen, graduated from St. John's College, and entered the diocesan seminary for the priesthood until ill health turned him to literature.

He edited the Catholic World first, assisted the Chicago Republican and the American Cyclopedia, and joined the New York Tribune as literary and musical critic. A partisan of the Wagner school, his letters on the Bayreuth festivals were among the first informative accounts of modern music in America. His impartial mind and pure, vigorous style advanced the highest musical art. He also wrote lives of Archbishop Hughes and Pius IX and a History of the United States for Catholic schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-shepherd:
John Shepherd was one of the great English church musicians of the sixteenth century, ranking with Tallis, Taverner, and Byrd. Born about 1512, he was educated at Saint Paul's music school under Thomas Mulliner. He became organist and master of the choristers at Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1542, and held a fellowship there from 1549 for two years.

In 1554, after twenty years as a music student, he petitioned Oxford for the doctorate in music. He served in Queen Mary's Chapel Royal from 1553 to 1558, giving three rolls of songs as a New Year's gift in 1557. Alive in 1562, he disappears from record after that date and is thought to have died or resigned in 1563. His surviving works include a five-voice Esurientes and Latin motets at the Royal College of Music. They include much church music at Oxford, including a delightful Magnificat praised by Hawkins and Morley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jules-mansard:
Jules Mansard was the French architect of Louis XIV's grand age. Born Jules Hardouin at Paris in 1646, grand-nephew of François Mansard, he took the Mansard name and won the king's favor, with titles, a count's rank, and charge of the royal buildings. Nearly all Louis' great works bear his name, fairly or not, for their cost.

His finest building is the Invalides church, whose dome rivals St. Paul's in London. Mansard built two domes, one over the other, so that paintings in the outer dome glow through an opening without glare. With Le Vau he finished Versailles, seeking sweep and space over pure beauty. He died at Marly in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurent-benar:
Laurent Benard (1573-1620) was the main founder of the Maurists, a Benedictine congregation. Born at Nevers, he joined the Cluniac Benedictines there and became a Sorbonne doctor. Later, as prior of Cluny College in Paris, he reformed it with two monks of the new Congregation of St. Vannes.

He turned down St. Etienne at Caen and Cluny's grand-priorship, made a second novitiate at St. Vannes, renewing his profession there in 1615. On his advice the Congregation of St. Maur took shape, meant to do for France what St. Vannes did for Lorraine. Royal letters patent followed in 1618, warmly backed by Cardinal de Retz and others. His Paris books of 1616 to 1619 include Pareneses, Instructions Monastiques, and Police reguliere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leon-menard:
Leon Menard (1706-1767) was a French writer and historian of Nimes. Born at Tarascon, he studied humanities under the Jesuits at Lyons, then law at Toulouse, and became counsellor of Nimes's Superior Court. From 1744 he lived constantly in Paris, busy with historical research, and his first work was a two-volume Histoire des Eveques de Nimes of 1737.

He then enlarged that work into the seven-volume Histoire Civile, Ecclesiastique et Litteraire de la ville de Nimes, published at Paris between 1758 and 1760 with illustrations. He also wrote Les Amours de Callisthene et de Chariclee and the widely read Moeurs et usages des Grecs of 1743. That work became a model for similar ones. He added articles on France in Roman times. In 1762 Avignon asked him to write its history, but ill health left it unfinished after two years. He belonged to the Academie des Inscriptions and other learned bodies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-baunard:
Louis Baunard was a French educator and rector of the Catholic University of Lille, born at Bellgarde in 1828. A priest of Orleans until 1877, he joined Lille first as professor, then as rector, and steered it through the freedom granted to higher education in 1875.

Backed by northern manufacturers, Lille turned out physicians, lawyers, businessmen, and priests trained to teach, with technical courses, economics, and popular extension lectures in factory towns. Baunard himself wrote on Plato's pedagogy, on saints John and Ambrose, and on founders like Louise de Marillac and Madame Barat, plus a survey of the nineteenth-century French Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrology-o:
Usuard was a Benedictine monk of St-Germain-des-Pres, Paris, who seems to have died about 875. At Charles the Bald's instigation he undertook his Martyrology, offering it in a prologue written very shortly before death. 

His Martyrologium, on which the existing Roman Martyrology depends very closely, stayed the Middle Ages' most famous document of its kind, surviving in countless manuscripts, partly listed by Dom Quentin in 1908. Its early medieval evolution, first accurately told by Quentin, is too tangled to detail here. Long known, though, is that Usuard mainly abridged Ado of Vienne's Martyrology into a form better fit for liturgical use. In some points he returned to a Lyonese recension of Bede's augmented Martyrology, ascribed to Archdeacon Florus. Dom Bouillant edited the text at Paris in 1718 from manuscript Latin 13745, dating from Usuard's time if not his autograph, and Du Sollier's Bollandist edition followed in Acta Sanctorum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-ward:
Mary Ward was a foundress, born 23 January 1585 and dead 23 January 1645. Eldest daughter of Marmaduke Ward and Ursula Wright, she was kin by blood to most great Yorkshire Catholic families. She entered St-Omer Poor Clares as a lay sister in 1606, founded a house for Englishwomen at Gravelines in 1607, but, not called to contemplation, resolved on active work.

The venture succeeded but, as a novelty, drew censure and opposition as well as praise. Pius V's rule demanding solemn vows and strict enclosure for women's communities blocked formal approbation, despite welcome from Archduchess Isabella, Elector Maximilian I, and Emperor Ferdinand II. Her work survived suppression, reviving along first lines, with rule approved by Clement XI in 1703 and institute by Pius IX in 1877. At Urban's wish she went to Rome, returned to England in 1639, and died at Heworth near York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-eber:
Trier bishop Matthias Eberhard (1815-1876) spent his life raising the learning and zeal of his clergy and people. Born at Trier, ordained in 1839, he served at Coblenz, became Bishop Arnoldi's secretary and then professor of dogmatics, and directed the Trier seminary from 1849 to 1862. He also sat in the Prussian Lower Chamber for the Catholic section from 1852 to 1856.

Named auxiliary bishop in 1862 and acknowledged as bishop in 1867, he pressed parish teaching, missions, retreats, and good people's libraries, and took St. Charles Borromeo as his model. At the Vatican Council he judged a definition of papal infallibility ill-timed, yet published it at once when passed. His stand against Prussia's Kulturkampf laws brought fines and prison at Trier through most of 1874, and grief at his diocese's plight hastened his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-alfor:
Michael Alford, a Jesuit missionary in England during the persecution, was born in London in 1587 and died at St. Omers on 11 August 1652. His true name was Griffith, and he sometimes passed as John Flood, aliases used to dodge detection. He entered the Louvain novitiate in 1607, studied philosophy at Seville's English College and theology at Louvain, and became a professed of the four vows in 1619.

After ordination he was sent to Naples to serve his countrymen there, plus British merchants and sailors using that port. From there he went to Rome, where he served as Penitentiary from 1615 to 1620. In 1628 he crossed to England and was seized at Dover at once as a priest. Freed, he went to Leicestershire, where he laboured nearly thirty-three years, hiding chiefly at Combe in Hereford, where a later search found a large library he likely used for his writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-hugue:
Benedictine scholar Nicolas-Hugues Ménard, a Maurist monk born at Paris in 1585, spent his life joining strict monastic living to deep study. He entered Saint-Denis in 1607 and joined the reform that became the Congregation of Saint-Maur. He preached widely in Paris and taught rhetoric for sixteen years at the College of Cluny.

Failing health sent him to Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where he worked in seclusion until his death in 1644. His books include a martyrology of Benedictine saints with added lives and notes, an edition of Benedict of Aniane's concord of rules, and writings on Saint Gregory the Great.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nithard:
Frankish historian Nithard, grandson of Charlemagne through his mother Bertha, wrote the insider's account of the Carolingian civil wars. A loyal man of Charles the Bald, he fought at Fontenoy in 841, went as envoy to Lothair in 840, and died fighting Normans around 843.

At Charles's request he wrote four books on the quarrels of Louis the Pious's sons, blaming Lothair's injustice in blunt but clear prose. The only lay historian of his age, Nithard reported what he saw and heard, and his body, found in the eleventh century, won a rhymed epitaph at Saint-Riquier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oliver-mailla:
Franciscan preacher Oliver Maillard, born in Brittany about 1430, preached blunt, popular Lenten sermons that spared neither people nor princes. Joining the Observants in Aquitaine, he became vicar provincial, then vicar general of the Ultramontane Observants in 1487, and was twice re-elected.

Fearless against the age's abuses, he attacked even Louis XI's cruelties. Miracles at his grave after his death at Toulouse in 1502 led Barcelona's chapter in 1508 to move his remains to a special chapel. His sermons, often rough in manner, won him lasting public veneration. He served as vicar general in three terms: 1487 to 1490, 1493 to 1496, and 1499 to 1502.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-c:
Our Lady of Charity of the Good Shepherd is a cloistered order. Its aim is refuge for girls and women of loose habits seeking penance and a Christian life. Voluntary penitents come, and so do those sent by civil or parental authority. Many penitents stay for life. They take vows as the magdalen class, an austere contemplative community under the Rule of the Third Order of Mount Carmel.

Children rescued from danger before they fell form a third class, the preservates, taught industry, self-respect, and duty. The three classes stay strictly apart. The sisters follow the Rule of Saint Augustine, with constitutions drawn largely from Saint Francis de Sales, and add a fourth vow to work for the conversion of penitents. After long opposition, Gregory XVI approved the Angers mother-house by brief of 3 April 1835.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oxford:
Oxford, one of England's oldest cities, grew beside a convent reportedly founded by Saint Frideswide as early as the eighth century. True history starts in 912, when Edward the Elder, King of the West Saxons, took the town. It was strongly walled against Danes, and again after the Norman Conquest, and castle keep, church tower, and wall fragments still witness its eleventh-century weight.

West of town rose castle and Oseney Abbey, northward stood Beaumont Palace, and the great church of Saint Frideswide rose under canons who followed the nuns. Henry II gave the citizens a charter matching London's privileges, and friars of many orders settled there. Parliaments often met in the city during the thirteenth century, and the entry traces its churches, religious houses, and civic growth into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-allard:
Paul Allard was a French archaeologist and historian born at Rouen on 15 September 1841. Admitted to the bar, he practised briefly at home and became a civil court judge, but literary and historical tastes pulled him from law to church history of the first four centuries. He wrote often for the Revue des Questions Historiques, editing it from 1904, and for other journals.

In 1874 he translated Northcote and Brownlow's Roma Sotterranea, adding much and enriching it with notes. Friendship with De Rossi and wide study led him to plan a history of Roman persecutions of Christians, on broad lines and with remarkable minuteness and finality. His Catholic sympathies, deep reading, mastery of catacomb archaeology, slave conditions, epigraphy, and Roman law fitted him to judge the delicate legal questions of church-state relations in the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-abelard:
Peter Abelard was a twelfth-century dialectician, philosopher, and theologian born at Pallet near Nantes in 1079. The eldest son of the village lord, he gave up arms for learning and wandered between the schools of Roscelin and others before reaching Paris. There he challenged William of Champeaux at the Cathedral School, then set up rival schools at Melun and Corbeil. This long Catholic Encyclopedia life follows a brilliant and stormy career.

Condemnation dogged him at Soissons in 1121 and again at Sens in 1141, where Bernard of Clairvaux pressed charges drawn from his writings. Between those trials he taught at the Paraclete and at St. Gildas de Rhuys. His works include the Sic et Non, which sets scriptural and patristic passages for and against disputed opinions without deciding them. He died in 1142.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-lombard:
Peter Lombard was an Irish archbishop who lived his episcopate in exile, born at Waterford about 1555. Schooled at Waterford and Westminster, where the historian Camden praised his gentleness and claimed him as a Protestant convert, he left Oxford for Louvain. There he shone in philosophy and theology, took a doctorate, was ordained, and became professor of theology.

Made provost of Cambrai cathedral in 1594, he went to Rome. There Clement VIII named him Archbishop of Armagh in 1601 and his own domestic prelate, giving him an income Ireland could not supply. He never reached Armagh. At Rome he presided for a time over the Congregatio de Auxiliis, judging Molina's work in the great dispute over predestination and grace. He died at Rome in 1625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-thomas:
Philip Thomas Howard was an English Dominican cardinal called the Cardinal of Norfolk, born at Arundel House in 1629. Third son of the Earl of Arundel, he joined the Dominicans in Italy at sixteen and professed at Rome in 1646 as Thomas. He preached a fervent address on England's conversion that moved his order's chapter to welcome English, Irish, and Scottish novices. Ordained in 1652, he founded Bornhem priory in Flanders with a college for English youths.

Under Charles II he served as grand almoner to Queen Catherine of Braganza at St. James's, on £500 a year. Made cardinal, he raised England's vicars apostolic from one to four, an arrangement lasting to 1840, and sat in three conclaves. He foresaw and regretted the crisis under James II, consoled that Bornhem lay beyond the new persecutors. He died at Rome in 1694, father and restorer of the English province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-bedard:
Pierre Bédard was a French Canadian lawyer and assemblyman, born at Charlesbourg near Quebec in 1762. Schooled at Quebec Seminary, he studied law, joined the bar, and sat in the Assembly from 1792 to 1812 for Northumberland, Quebec's lower town, and Surrey. Constitutional questions absorbed him above all, a field many officials grasped only imperfectly.

When Le Canadien appeared in 1806 he wrote warmly for constitutional government, and Governor Craig suppressed the paper in spring 1810 and jailed Bédard. He stayed some twelve months, refusing freedom offers that would seat him without trial, demanding a regular hearing the authorities would not grant, and leaving at last for peace's sake. Governor Prevost then named him judge at Three Rivers in 1813 as compensation, a post he held until illness ended it in 1827. He died in 1829.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-biard:
Pierre Biard was a Jesuit missionary to Acadia, born at Grenoble in 1576. Called from a Lyons chair in scholastic theology and Hebrew, he waited three years against Calvinist opposition before sailing with Edmond Massé in January 1611, reaching Port Royal on Pentecost Day. A predecessor's indiscriminate baptisms, hostile colonists, and a failing business made progress slight.

Madame de Guercheville then sent La Saussaye to found Saint Sauveur at today's Bar Harbor in 1613. Samuel Argall of Virginia plundered it at once and carried Biard toward Jamestown. Storms drove the captors' ship to the Azores and Wales, where Biard saved its captain from hanging as a pirate. Back in France he faced abuse as a supposed traitor, was vindicated by Champlain, never returned to Canada, and ended life as a famous southern missionary and army chaplain. He died at Avignon in 1622.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-de-ron:
Pierre de Ronsard was the prince of French Renaissance poets, born at La Poissonnière near Vendôme in September 1524. Tutored at home, then sent to Navarre College at nine, he left before graduating to serve as page to the Duke of Orléans and to James V of Scotland. Three years in Scotland and England made him fluent in English, and he travelled Germany and Piedmont before incurable deafness retired him from public life in 1541.

Seven years of study under the Greek scholar Dorat at Coqueret followed, with ambition to find new paths for French poetry. His Odes of 1550 and Amours de Cassandre won him the title Prince of Poets. Six editions of his works appeared between 1560 and 1584, including the Hymnes and the unfinished Franciade of 1572. He enriched French vocabulary and invented metres. He died at Saint-Cosme priory in 1585.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-gustav:
Pierre Gustave Toutant Beauregard was a Confederate general, born near New Orleans on 28 May 1818. Appointed to West Point, he graduated in 1838 and passed from artillery to engineers. He served in Mexico at Vera Cruz, Cerro Gordo, Contreras, Chapultepec, and Mexico City, wounded twice in September 1847 and brevetted major.

West Point superintendent in January 1861, he resigned almost at once and joined the Confederacy. Commanding at Charleston, he opened the Civil War by attacking Fort Sumter, then led Confederate forces at Bull Run on 21 July 1861. Second to A. S. Johnston at Shiloh, he succeeded him when Johnston fell and nearly routed Grant's army on the first day. After leave for failing health, he held Charleston against siege for a year and a half, joined Lee at Petersburg in 1864, and surrendered with J. E. Johnston in April 1865. Afterwards he served as Louisiana's adjutant-general. He died at New Orleans in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-mignar:
Pierre Mignard was a French painter who dominated fashionable portraiture in Rome and Paris in the seventeenth century. He was born at Troyes in 1612 and first meant for medicine. He trained at Bourges and Fontainebleau, joined Simon Vouet's Paris studio, and then spent twenty-two years in Rome. There he copied the Carracci frescoes and learned from Venetian colour.

In Rome he painted princes, cardinals, and three popes. His many graceful Madonnas, nicknamed mignardes, won him a huge following. Later critics found them polished rather than deeply devout. Back in France he rose to the top of his profession, and the entry weighs his skill at pleasing patrons against the limits of his religious feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-paul-r:
Pierre-Paul Royer-Collard was a French philosopher and politician who defended both liberty and the Bourbon monarchy. He was born at Sompuis in 1763 and practised law. He sat in the Council of the Five Hundred in 1797 demanding freedom for the Catholic religion. He was driven out after the coup of 18 Fructidor.

Under Napoleon he took the philosophy chair at the Sorbonne in 1809. He taught a commonsense spiritualism against the materialism of the previous century. After the Restoration he led the doctrinaires, a middle party, and presided over the Chamber. In 1830 he presented the address of the 221 deputies that refused the ministry of Polignac.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-menard:
René Ménard, missionary, was born at Paris in 1604 and died about 10 August 1661 in what is now Wisconsin. After his studies he sailed from Dieppe at the beginning of May 1640, and on reaching Quebec he was assigned to the Hurons, labouring first among the Nippisriens. After the Huron missions were destroyed, he went to Three Rivers, and on 17 May he set out for the Iroquois country.

Sent to the Cayugas, he was brutally treated for the first two months, then won their affection. When the Iroquois missions were interrupted, he returned to Three Rivers, but in 1659, aged fifty-five, he started with three hundred Ottawas for the Far West. The post he tried to found was probably at Keweenaw, a hundred leagues west of Sault Sainte Marie, where his sufferings form one of the most pathetic pages of the missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-gerar:
Richard Gerard was an English Catholic gentleman whose loyalty to persecuted priests cost him his freedom and his life. Born about 1635 into a Staffordshire family that had grown rich under Elizabeth, he himself became a Catholic by a path the entry cannot trace. He befriended Jesuit missioners, sent three sons to their college at St-Omer, and acted as trustee for small properties on their behalf.

His downfall came during the panic over the Popish Plot. Having attended a harmless gathering at Boscobel, where Charles II had once hidden in an oak tree, Gerard stepped forward to defend accused Catholic lords. The informer Stephen Dugdale then accused him of funding plotters and plotting the king's murder. Thrown into Newgate in 1679, he waited ten months without trial and died there in March 1680, attended in his last hours by a Jesuit priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-guerar:
Robert Guerard was a Maurist monk and biblical scholar whose exile led to a notable manuscript find. Born at Rouen in 1641, he worked at Saint-Denys on the Maurist edition of St Augustine's works. In 1675 the king ordered him away, wrongly suspecting him of a hand in L'Abbe commendataire, a work that attacked the holding of abbeys in commendam.

His superior sent him to Notre Dame at Ambronay. While in exile he found, at the Carthusian house of Portes, a manuscript of Augustine's Opus imperfectum against Julian of Eclanum. That text later served the Maurist edition. Recalled after a year, he spent the rest of his life at Fecamp and Saint-Ouen. His own biblical work, an abridged Bible in familiar questions and answers, appeared at Rouen in 1707. He died at Saint-Ouen in 1715.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-guisca:
Robert Guiscard was the Norman adventurer who founded the kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Born about 1016, eldest son of Tancred's second marriage, he left Normandy in 1046 with five horsemen and thirty foot soldiers to join brothers already serving Lombard princes against Byzantium. Tall, broad, blond, and deep-voiced, he earned the nickname Guiscard, or Wiseacre, for crafty shrewdness.

Rebuffed at first by his brother Drogo, he lived for a time by brigandage from San Marco, raiding Byzantine posts, monasteries, and travellers. Marriage to Aubree, kinswoman of a Norman chief, gave him two hundred horsemen and a settled base. He fought at Civitella in 1053, where Pope Leo IX was captured. Elected Norman leader in 1057, he bent the chiefs to his will, set his brother Roger in Calabria, and allied with Pope Nicholas II in 1059. He died in 1085.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rockford:
Rockford is a diocese in northwestern Illinois, created on 23 September 1908 from the Archdiocese of Chicago. It takes in twelve counties, from Jo Daviess to Kendall, covering 6,867 square miles. Its Catholic population was 50,000, mostly Irish and Germans or their descendants, out of 414,872 people in total. The city of Rockford, a manufacturing centre, had 48,000 people.

Peter James Muldoon, formerly auxiliary bishop of Chicago, was appointed first bishop and took possession of his see on 15 December 1908. Figures for 1911 list 99 secular priests and 18 missions with 3,850 attendants. They list five hospitals, a maternity home, a home for the aged, and Mt St Mary's Academy for Girls at St Charles with 84 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hildega:
Hildegard, born at Böckelheim on the Nahe in 1098 and dead at Rupertsberg near Bingen in 1179, was a great seer and prophetess known as the Sibyl of the Rhine. Her family name is unknown, though early biographers name her parents Hildebert and Mechtildis and describe their nobility and wealth. A weak and sickly child, she got little schooling at home. Her parents, who had promised her to God's service, placed her at eight under Jutta, a recluse at Disibodenberg.

There she learned to read and sing the Latin psalms well enough for the daily office, but she never learned to write. After taking the Benedictine habit and making her profession, she became superior when Jutta died in 1136. She later moved her community to Rupertsberg near Bingen in 1147 or 1148 with eighteen sisters, and probably founded a second convent at Eibingen about 1165.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-theodar:
Theodard, archbishop of Narbonne, was born at Montauban about 840 and died there on 1 May 893. From a noble and wealthy family, he studied church and secular learning with zeal. As a subdeacon he impressed a synod at Toulouse that was settling a dispute between the local Jews and Bishop Bernhard. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a careful administrator of a troubled see.

Archbishop Sigebod thought so highly of him that he made him archdeacon, where Theodard won praise as eyes to the blind and father to the poor. Elected Sigebod's successor in 885 and consecrated that August, he travelled to Rome for the pallium in 886 and defended his suffragan dioceses, repairing damage from war and disorder. The entry paints a pastor whose charity matched his firmness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salford:
Salford, an English diocese erected on 29 September 1850, covers the hundreds of Salford and Blackburn in Lancashire, including the mill towns of Manchester, Salford, Blackburn, Oldham, Bury, Burnley, and Rochdale. Its area matches the old Catholic deanery of Manchester, but it took Salford's name so as not to offend Protestants, since an Anglican Manchester see had appeared in 1847. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a careful piece of naming.

Pius IX first gave Salford the hundred of Leyland as well, but a brief of 27 June 1851 moved Leyland, with the Catholic town of Preston, to Liverpool. Blackburn hundred stretches twenty-four miles east to west across the north-west of the diocese. The entry lists bishops, parishes, and institutions, showing a church serving the factory towns of industrial Lancashire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-clo:
Clonard, Irish Cluain Eraird, Erard's Meadow, stood on the Boyne at the border of Ireland's northern and southern halves. Its school, the most famous of the sixth century, was founded by Finnian, abbot and wonder-worker born at Myshall in Carlow about 470. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a teacher who studied in Wales and returned home.

Placed young under Fortchern, Finnian crossed to Wales to perfect holiness and learning under its great saints, staying thirty years by the Salamanca manuscript's account. Home again, he preached, taught, and founded churches from place to place until an angel led him to Clonard, his promised place of resurrection. There he built a cell and a church of clay and wattle, later replaced in stone, and lived in study, mortification, and prayer as fame gathered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-red:
Sebastian Redford was born on 27 April 1701 and died on 2 January 1763. Schooling at St Omer, Watten, and Liège came first; he then joined the Jesuits. He served as chaplain to the Wrights of Kelvedon and then the Herberts of Powis from 1733 to 1748. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a chaplain of the penal years.

The second Marquess of Powis, who died in 1745, trusted Redford much, but the third was unfriendly. When the third died in 1748 a Protestant succeeded, the chaplaincy lapsed, and Redford, as he put it, had to rue the ruin of his former flock. Moved to Croxteth, Lord Molyneux's seat, he published An Important Inquiry on church reform in 1751. Excise officers seized and destroyed 400 copies, half the edition, and an enlarged second edition followed in 1758.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sicard:
Sicard, Bishop of Cremona in Italy in the twelfth century, came from one of the city's leading families and died in 1215. After studies in several cities, he was made subdeacon by Lucius III in 1182, returned home, and was ordained priest by Bishop Offredus, whom he succeeded in 1185. The Holy See trusted him with many important missions, and he enjoyed the confidence of Emperor Frederick I.

His fame rests on three works. His Chronicon sums up world history to 1213 and throws light on Frederick's crusade. His Mitrale, in nine books, treats the liturgy and church offices. His Summa Canonum handbooks canon law on the basis of the so-called Decretum Gelasianum. The entry marks him as historian, canonist, and liturgiologist in equal measure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of the Incarnate Word, a congregation with simple vows, began through Bishop Claude Marie Dubuis of Galveston. In 1866 he travelled to France seeking religious willing to serve works of mercy in his large Texas diocese. He approached Mother Angelique, superior of a Lyons convent, and the first sisters came to care for the sick.

Other bands trained and professed at Lyons joined them in 1867 and 1868, perfecting old works and starting new ones. On 31 March 1869 Dubuis sent a colony to found a convent at San Antonio, erected as an independent centre in 1870. Before 1874 the sisters cared only for the sick, aged, and orphans. Their works later grew to academies, schools, orphanages, hospitals, and homes for the aged across Texas, Missouri, Oklahoma, and Mexico.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded at Steyl, near Tegelen, Holland, in 1875 by Arnold Janssen during the Kulturkampf, the Society of the Divine Word was the first German Catholic missionary society. It serves pagan nations through priests and lay brothers, who take three-year vows after a year's novitiate and perpetual vows before ordination. Its first mission opened in 1882 in southern Shantung, China, a district holding 158 Catholics among about 10,000,000 non-Christians.

By 1906 to 1907 that mission counted 35,378 Catholics and 36,367 catechumens, with 46 European and 12 Chinese priests. A second mission in Togo, West Africa, begun in 1892 with scarcely a hundred Catholics, counted 3,300 Catholics and 68 mission stations by 1906. A third mission in German New Guinea, begun in 1896, faced over a hundred languages in its district and counted 1,000 native Catholics by 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adalard:
St. Adalard, born about 751 and dead on 2 January 827, was a Carolingian prince turned monk, and this entry traces a career spent between court and cloister. Son of Bernard, son of Charles Martel and half-brother of Pepin. And cousin-german to Charlemagne, he learned at the palace school, became Count of the Palace while young, and entered Corbie in Picardy at twenty.

Seeking deeper seclusion at Monte Cassino, he was ordered back to Corbie, elected abbot, and made prime minister to Pepin's son, King of Italy. Suspected of backing Bernard's bid for the imperial crown in 814, Louis the Pious banished him to Noirmoutier for seven years, then recalled him as chief adviser. And with his brother Wala he founded New Corvey in Westphalia in 822.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernward:
St. Bernward, thirteenth bishop of Hildesheim in Germany, was born about the middle of the tenth century. He died on 20 November 1022. This entry follows a boy of a noble Saxon family, counting distinguished men of Church and State among its members. His grandfather was Athelbero, count palatine of Saxony. Losing his parents while still young, he came under the care of his uncle Volkmar, bishop of Utrecht. Volkmar entrusted his education to Thangmar, the pious and learned director of the Heidelberg cathedral school.

Under Thangmar, Bernward progressed rapidly in Christian piety, in the sciences, and in the liberal and even mechanical arts. He became proficient in mathematics, painting, architecture, and particularly in making ecclesiastical vessels and ornaments of silver and gold. He finished his studies at Mainz, where Archbishop Willigis, chancellor of the empire from 975 to 1011, ordained him priest. The entry follows him on to the bishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gerard:
Gerard of Brogne, soldier turned reformer, replaced lax clerics with true monks in the houses he touched. Born at Staves in Namur late in the ninth century, he was son of Stance of a ducal house and Plectrude, sister of Stephen of Liège. He first followed arms, pious amid camp distractions. He enlarged a family chapel at Brogne into a large church. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Brogne to 3 October 959.

Sent about 917 by Namur's count on a mission to Robert, brother of King Eudes, he lodged his followers at Paris while he lived at St-Denis. Struck by the monks' lives, he took the habit with count and uncle's consent and was ordained priest after eleven years. Returning to Brogne, he replaced lax clerics with monks animated by true observance, beginning a reformer's career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-godard:
Godard, bishop of Hildesheim from 1021 to 1038, reformed abbeys across Germany before he reformed a diocese. Born about 960 near Altaich in Upper Bavaria, he studied long, took the Benedictine habit in 991, and rose swiftly to prior, then abbot, of Altaich. Rigorous observance marked his rule, and his fitness for reform carried him to Hersfeld in Hesse, Tegernsee near Freising, and Kremsmünster near Passau. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 4 May 1038.

On Bernard of Hildesheim's death in 1021, Godard was chosen successor, yielding only to Emperor Henry II's urgent admonitions. His zeal and prudence kept up the high tradition of his cloistered work in his new see. Canonized by Innocent II in 1131, he stands in the entry as a monk whose discipline travelled: from one abbey's observance to a reformer's circuit, then to a bishop's throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-margaret-w:
Margaret Ward, martyr of Tyburn, smuggled a rope to an imprisoned priest and paid for it with her life. Born at Congleton in Cheshire and executed at Tyburn on 30 August 1588, she was of good family. She dwelt for a time with a lady of distinction named Whitall, then living in London. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 preserves her story in brief.

Learning that William Watson, priest and author of the Quodlibets, was imprisoned, she obtained leave to visit him. After several visits she got past the gaoler's vigilance and furnished Watson with a cord for escape. At the appointed time the boatman engaged to carry the priest downriver refused, and the plot unravelled into arrest and execution. Nothing is known of her early life beyond family and London lodging, but the entry fixes her deed: visits, a cord, a boatman, and a martyr's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-of-:
Thomas of Hereford, also Cantelupe, combined learning, royal service, and episcopal reform in thirteenth-century England. Born at Hambledon about 1218 to William de Cantelupe and Millicent de Gournay, he was schooled by his uncle Walter, bishop of Worcester, at Oxford and Paris. At Lyons in 1245 he became a papal chaplain.

Back at Oxford, he taught canon law and was elected university chancellor in 1262. In the Barons' Wars he took the popular side, pleaded the barons' case before Louis IX at Amiens in 1263, and served as chancellor of England after Lewes. Exiled after Montfort's fall, he lectured at Paris, then resumed at Oxford. Bishop of Hereford from 1275, he reformed his diocese and clashed with Archbishop Peckham. He died at Orvieto on 25 August 1282.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-willibrord:
Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht and apostle of the Frisians, built the Dutch Church from Echternach. Son of Wilgils, born in Northumbria in 658, he studied at Ripon under Wilfrid, then entered the Benedictine order. At twenty he went to Ireland, spending twelve years at Rathmelsigi under Egbert, who gave him and eleven companions the Frisian mission at Pepin's request.

They reached Utrecht but moved to Pepin's court. In 692 Willibrord went to Rome for apostolic authorisation, and at Pepin's wish returned in 695 to be consecrated bishop of the Frisians by Sergius, taking the name Clement, with the pallium. He founded a monastery at Utrecht, built the Holy Redeemer as his cathedral, and in 698 established Echternach abbey. He died there on 7 November 739.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-brethren-:
Persons called the brethren of the Lord in the New Testament pose two lasting puzzles, and this entry takes both head on. Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, and Paul all name them. Matthew chapter 13 and Mark chapter 6 list four by name: James, Joseph or Joses, Simon, and Jude, with sisters also mentioned. The casual way the names appear suggests the list is not complete.

James stands beyond doubt as bishop of Jerusalem and author of the first Catholic Epistle. Whether James, Jude, and Simon match the apostles of those names, and what exact kinship bound them to Jesus, remain disputed. Cousins, half-brothers, and full brothers all find advocates, and the entry weighs the evidence for each reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodat-gabri:
Recollect lay brother, missionary, and historian Theodat-Gabriel Sagard is the Canadian pioneer sketched here. Born in France near the sixteenth century's end, dying near the seventeenth's close, he sailed to Canada in 1623 with Nicolas Viel, future martyr, for the Huron mission. Anne of Austria supplied a portable altar and vestments for their journey.

Joseph Le Caron, his superior, taught him first rudiments of the difficult Huron tongue en route, so Sagard began catechising and baptising on arrival. Hardships abounded, mass wine failed, and wild grape juice served instead. One year's residence won neophytes' affection and ascendancy, before a 1624 Quebec provisioning trip and a superior's recall to France cut his mission short.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-coun:
Swiss Catholic writer and statesman Theodore von Scherer-Boccard fought for Church freedom with his pen. Born at Dornach in Solothurn on 12 May 1816, he died at Solothurn on 6 February 1885. A good Solothurn family raised him, he learned at the town school and lyceum, then read law at Fribourg's Jesuit college. He came home to journalism.

His paper Die Schildwache am Jura, begun in 1836, backed Church freedom and the rights of the people, and a news bureau followed in 1839. A seat on the cantonal council from 1838 brought clashes with the government, and in 1841 he lived for a time in Alsace and Paris. Lucerne then asked him to launch the Staatszeitung der katholischen Schweiz, the chief voice of Swiss Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ward:
Thomas Ward, a controversial writer born at Danby Castle, Yorkshire, in 1652, turned from Presbyterian schooling to Catholic apologetics. The son of a farmer, he was educated at Pickering School, worked as a private tutor, and was led by his studies to become a Catholic. He toured France and Italy and served five or six years in the papal guard, fighting against the Turks.

Returning to England at James II's accession in 1688, he threw his learning into controversy. His most popular work, England's Reformation, a poem in four cantos in the metre of Hudibras, appeared posthumously in 1710. His Errata to the Protestant Bible, first published in 1688 and often reprinted, drew a defence from Bishop Milner. He died at St. Germain, France, in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Oxford's fabulous antiquity fills the opening of this entry, only to be set aside. The fifteenth-century chronicler Rous traced it to the days when Samuel judged Israel, while a writer of Edward III's reign had philosophers founding it after Brutus and the Trojans seized Albion. The most durable fiction, heard from the mid-fourteenth century into the nineteenth, made King Alfred its founder. The truth is that no approximate date can be assigned to the growth of schools into a university.

The entry follows that real growth: masters gathering, colleges founded, quarrels with town and crown, and the slow building of faculties and libraries. It covers the Reformation's shock, the seventeenth-century troubles, and later reforms. Readers get a sober history that clears away legend and shows how Oxford became Oxford, step by step, without a founding moment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-miles-ger:
Miles Gerard was a martyr born about 1550 at Wigan, executed at Rochester on 13 April 1590, or 30 April by another reckoning. Perhaps sprung from the Gerards of Ince, he tutored the children of Squire Edward Tyldesley at Morleys in Lancashire about 1576. From there in 1579 he moved to the Douai and Reims seminaries, took ordination on 7 April 1583, and remained as professor until 31 August 1589.

On that date he started for England with five companions. At Dunkirk sailors would take only two passengers, so the missioners cast lots for precedence, and Gerard and Francis Dicconson, seemingly eldest and youngest of the party, won. Bound for London, they were driven off course into Dover harbour, where they were examined and arrested on suspicion in November. The entry follows their trial and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-philip-ho:
Philip Howard was a martyr and Earl of Arundel, born at Arundel House in London on 28 June 1557, who died in the Tower of London on 19 October 1595. His grandfather was Henry, Earl of Surrey, the poet Henry VIII executed in 1547, and his father Thomas, Duke of Norfolk, whom Elizabeth executed in 1572. He counted Philip II of Spain, then King of England, among his godfathers.

His father, who had conformed to the state religion, had him taught partly by John Foxe, the Protestant martyrologist, and later sent him to Cambridge. His father married as his third wife Elizabeth, widow of Lord Dacre, and matched her three heiress daughters to his three sons. Anne, Philip's wife, Countess of Arundel and Surrey, survived to 1630, a woman of remarkable generosity and courage who, after her conversion, patronized Father Southwell. The entry follows Philip's own conversion, imprisonment, and death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-h:
William Howard, Viscount Stafford, was a Catholic nobleman beheaded on Tower Hill in December 1680. Born in 1614, grandson of Philip Howard, Earl of Arundel, he was made a Knight of the Bath at Charles I's coronation and married Mary, sister of the last Baron Stafford. The Stafford title was revived for him in 1640, and he became a viscount.

After his father's death, bitter lawsuits over the impoverished Howard estates entangled him for years, with relatives and their agents pursuing him even abroad. He was twice arrested and acquitted with honour. Named first on Titus Oates's list of Catholic lords to be proscribed, he was committed to the Tower in October 1678 and tried before the House of Lords. Condemned by 55 votes to 31 on perjured evidence, he met death with quiet dignity, and his confessor praised his generosity, charity, and love of justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-w:
William Ward, whose real name was Webster, was a priest executed at Tyburn in July 1641. Born at Thornby in Westmorland about 1560, he was over forty when he went to Douai to train for the priesthood, and was ordained in 1608. Bound for England, he was driven ashore in Scotland, arrested, and imprisoned for three years.

Once free, he laboured in England for thirty years, twenty of them spent in various prisons as a confessor for the faith. Fiery and exacting as a spiritual director, he drew many penitents, and his secret charities were so hidden that he was even accused of miserliness. When Parliament proclaimed in April 1641 that all priests must leave under pain of death, he refused to retire. Arrested in his nephew's house, he was condemned at the Old Bailey and suffered on the feast of St Anne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-pie:
Pierre-Julien Eymard was the French founder of the Society of the Blessed Sacrament, a congregation devoted to honouring the Eucharist, the consecrated bread and wine of Mass. Born at La Mure in 1811, he entered the Oblates of Mary in 1829 but illness sent him home. He was ordained from the Grenoble seminary in 1834, later joining the Marists and becoming their provincial in 1845.

His whole spiritual life centred on the Eucharist, the theme of his sermons and the object of his worship. On pilgrimage to Fourvières in 1851 he promised to found a congregation of priests whose chief duty would be adoration of the Blessed Sacrament. Starting in a small Paris house with a single companion in 1857. The community won a blessing from Pius IX and spread rapidly to Rome, Belgium, Holland, Spain, Canada, the United States, and South America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-tho:
Thomas Pilchard, or Pilcher, was a Sussex priest executed at Dorchester in March 1587. Born at Battle in 1557, he became a fellow of Balliol College, Oxford, in 1576 and took his M. A. in 1579. Reaching Reims in 1581, he was ordained at Laon in 1583 and sent to England, where he was arrested, banished, and returned almost at once.

Arrested again in early March 1587 and held in Dorchester gaol, he converted thirty people in the fortnight between committal and condemnation. Dragged so cruelly on the hurdle that he fainted on reaching the scaffold, he stood erect when the rope was cut, still alive. The executioner, a cook, performed his office so clumsily that Pilchard turned to the sheriff and asked, in effect, whether this was his justice. Father Warford counted him unmatched in virtue among western priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-byrd:
William Byrd was the leading English composer of his age and a steadfast Catholic under two Protestant monarchs. Born in London in 1542 or 1543, he died 4 July 1623. A musician's son, he learned under Thomas Tallis, played at Lincoln Cathedral from 1563, joined the Chapel Royal in 1570, and gained its organist title in 1575. Fétis dubbed him the English Palestrina for his mastery of counterpoint, the weaving of independent voice lines.

Byrd pioneered the English madrigal, a short part-song form from Italy, and wrote a huge body of virginal music still played. His church works matter most: gradualia for the church year in 1607, and Psalms, Songs and Sonnets in 1611. Parthenia with Bull and Gibbons, and three masses for three, four, and five voices complete the list. Two motets, Domine, ne irascaris and Civitas sancti tui, remain in Anglican use. His will prayed to die a true member of the Catholic Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-cliff:
William Clifford, alias Mansell, was an English priest and devotional writer who shunned high office out of humility. He died on 30 April 1670. Son of Henry Clifford and Elizabeth Thimelby, he never pressed his claim to the Barony of Cumberland. After schooling and ordination at Douai, he joined the English mission. As vice-president he steered the English College at Lisbon through hard times, then led Tournay College at Paris, assigned by Cardinal Richelieu to English clergy.

Clifford dodged a bishopric in 1660 and turned down the Douai presidency in 1670, ending his days in the Hôpital des Incurables at Paris. His books include Christian Rules Proposed to a Vertuous Soule of 1615, a translation of The Spirituall Combat of 1656, and the Little Manual of Poore Man's Dayly Devotion, often reprinted. Two further works on kings and controversy survive in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-georg:
William George Ward was an English writer and convert whose logic pushed the Oxford Movement toward Rome. Born in London in 1812, he died in 1882. Schooled at Winchester and Christ Church, Oxford, he took a second class in letters and mathematics in 1834, won a Lincoln scholarship, and became a Balliol fellow and tutor. A keen mathematician and deep philosopher, he swayed students through debate and through classes that often turned into religious argument.

At first Ward followed Dr Arnold and scorned the Tractarians, but in 1838 he joined Newman's party with fervour. He defended Tract XC in pamphlets and pressed for slow absorption of Catholic doctrine toward reunion. His Ideal of a Christian Church of 1844 earned him the tag Ideal Ward. Stripped of his degrees on 13 February 1845, he saw no honest place left in the Establishment and submitted to the Catholic Church in September 1845.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-giffa:
William Giffard was the second Norman Bishop of Winchester, serving from 1100 to 1129 through the investiture quarrel. Little is known before his bishopric beyond posts as canon and dean of Rouen and chancellor to William the Conqueror, William Rufus, and Henry I. When Henry took the throne at Winchester in August 1100, his first goodwill act was to fill the see, vacant since 1098, with Giffard, then still only a deacon.

Giffard grasped at once that king versus Church over appointments belonged to Europe's great investiture fight, and he refused the pastoral staff from royal hands. Henry, needing churchmen's backing, let him take the see's lands without it. After exile, a conscience stand at a consecration, and travel to Rome with Saint Anselm, compromise came in 1107: homage stayed, but ring and crosier passed from the king's gift. Anselm consecrated Giffard on 11 August 1107.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-giffo:
William Gifford was an English priest who rose from exile student to Archbishop of Reims. Born in Hampshire in 1554, he died at Reims in 1629. Son of John Gifford of Weston-under-Edge, he entered Oxford in 1569 under a Catholic tutor, then moved to Louvain in 1573 and took a master's degree. He studied theology under Bellarmine before unrest drove him on to Paris, Reims, and the English College at Rome.

Ordained in March 1582, Allen recalled him to teach theology at Reims, where he worked nearly twelve years and took a doctorate at Pont-à-Mousson in 1584. He served as Allen's chaplain at Rome, held the Lille deanery for about ten years, and led Reims University as rector magnificus. In 1608 he took Benedictine habit, became prior at Dieulouard, founded a house at Saint Malo, and was consecrated coadjutor at Reims in 1618.
cranford:
Elizabeth Cleghorn Gaskell set her novel Cranford in a small English town ruled, as the first chapter says, by Amazons: genteel widows and spinsters with little money and strict manners. The narrator, Mary Smith, visits from the manufacturing town of Drumble and reports their teas, calls, and small economies. This illustrated edition carries twenty-five coloured pictures by C E Brock.

Chapters follow Miss Matty Jenkyns and her circle through an old love affair, the arrival of Captain Brown, a conjurer's visit, a bank failure, and the return of a long-lost brother. Gaskell treats these small events with humor and tenderness. The result is a gentle classic about friendship, pride, and making do.
devil-s-ford:
Bret Harte set Devil's Ford in a California mining camp enjoying a season of unequalled prosperity along the North Fork. The partners of the claim, the Kearney brothers, Dick Mattingly, and Maryland Joe among them, plan like princes while wearing patched breeches. They vote money for statues, fountains fed by a ditch twenty miles away, a town hall, and a free library, all from gold not yet dug.

Harte lets their boyish delight run while the camp's single street fills with new cabins and old habits persist beside prospecting pans full of gold. A water scheme to work the claim properly drives the plot toward the usual Harte reckoning, where fortune tests character. Greed, loyalty, and luck share the diggings.
doe-osti-2572786-compare-low-gain-1d-and: Low-gain X-ray laser oscillator models got compared, and this DOE report pits 1D against 3D. The pages detail the storage-ring study. The photon scientists get their verdict. The models were low-gain. The study was storage-ring.
doe-osti-2999890-real-time-in-line-monit: Hanford tank wastes got real-time monitoring, and this DOE year-one report covers in-line sensors. The pages detail the findings. The waste folks get their data. The monitoring was real-time in-line. The report was year one.
doe-osti-3001734-electric-utility-commun: Utility comms standards got their 2025 landscape, and this DOE edition maps the electric sector. The pages detail the standards. The utilities get their guide. The edition was 2025. The guide was utility. The standards were detailed. The sector was electric. The edition was guide.
doe-osti-3383764-coalition-for-community: C2SAGES got geothermal-coalitioned, and this DOE text covers affordable systems. The pages detail the supported findings. The energy folks get their data. The energy was community-supported. The data were energy. The C2SAGES were systems. The affordable were geothermal.
doe-osti-3685163-cathodic-protection-mod: Hanford tanks got cathodic-modeled, and this DOE text covers double-shell protection. The pages detail the cathodic findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The farms were tank. The data were nuclear. The underground were tank. The double-shell were farms.
doe-osti-3874824-real-time-in-line-monit: Hanford wastes got real-time-monitored, and this DOE monitoring covers in-line tank wastes. The pages detail the real findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The time was real. The data were nuclear. The tank were wastes. The in-line were monitoring.
evolution-of-life-and-form-four-lectures:
Besant's Evolution of Life and Form gathers four lectures on theosophical evolution. Annie Besant delivered them at the twenty-third anniversary meeting of the Theosophical Society. The meeting sat at Adyar, Madras, in 1898. This second edition is dated 1900, and the record lists 1909.

The lectures run in a set order across four mornings. Ancient and Modern Science opens the series, then Functions of the Gods. Evolution of Life comes third, and Evolution of Form closes it. Besant warns her hearers that the theme is complex and hard. She treats her audience as students, not casual listeners. Technical terms, she argues, serve precision for the prepared mind. The lectures join Eastern thought with claims about life's unfolding.
father-stafford:
Hope's Father Stafford is a novel of a clergyman caught in a country-house circle. Anthony Hope also wrote The Prisoner of Zenda. This Chicago and New York edition is dated 1895. Fifteen chapters carry the tale from Eugene Lane's house party onward.

Eugene Lane opens the book as a fortunate young man. Youth, health, a seat in Parliament, and a beauty's promised hand are his. Sir Roderick Ayre pities him for his father's workhouse start. New faces and old feuds fill the second chapter. Father Stafford changes his habits in the third. Later chapters bring a vigil, a retreat, and the Battle of Baden. Waiting Lady Claudia's Pleasure turns the love plot. Hope mixes clerical crisis with society comedy.
five-thousand-dollars-reward:
Pinkerton opens a dime novel with a tramp at a cottage door in Five Thousand Dollars Reward, printed in 1886. A. Frank Pinkerton sets his tale in a country village. The tramp begs a glass of water from a pretty girl at her door. Her brother Ransom, she says, will be around soon. The tramp's eyes glitter as he reads her face. The frontispiece gives the game away: an arrest for the murder of Victoria Vane.

The sampled pages pass to a warning. A young man named Bordine finds a note that had been fixed to his door. It bids him be ever on the alert: a conspiracy has been formed for his destruction. Silas Keene, it says, has already fallen, and Bordine is marked. The note is signed only A Friend. Murder, reward, and pursuit drive the tale in the brisk Pinkerton style.
frank-merriwell-s-reward:
Standish opens this Merriwell novel with a runaway automobile scattering Frank's crowd. Harry Rattleton twists his warning words, Bart Hodge straightens them, and Dismal Jones blames Satan for new-fangled inventions. Frank steps in as the machine bears down.

A darker thread runs beneath the fun. Pike lays a circumstantial tale before Fairfax Lee: boat-keeper Barney Lynn lured a man onto a steamer for robbery, after the fellow drank himself helpless at Joe Connelly's saloon. Lee knows Connelly's is among the worst dens of the city. Burt L. Standish published Frank Merriwell's Reward in 1900.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BastRichard_Bas: A declassified US government document titled for Richard Bast, via the Internet Archive. Beyond the title's name, the record is empty: no year, no source office, no summary. The underlying text has not been found publicly. It stands as a name on file and little more.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BeckerEdward_Be: FBI Memorandum Routing Slip: the bureau's routing slip circulated among officials including Cartha DeLoach and John Mohr. The bureaucracy's paper trail, complete, for researchers of the files. A single slip. A US government document from the archive.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrowderEdward_B: FBI Identification Record, April 25, 1942: the bureau's identification record - number 4 840 823 - furnished for official use only. Wartime paperwork, complete, for researchers and readers. A single record, filed. A public record. A US government document from the archive.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CrawfordCliffor:
Harold Weisberg wrote on March 14, 1971 to Clifford Crawford of the Galloway School in Atlanta. The immediate business was practical: getting Crawford a copy of Weisberg's unpublished work. From there the letter moves into the cases that occupied Weisberg's research.

Weisberg discusses the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. and the case of Fred Hampton and Mark Clark, the Black Panthers killed in a Chicago police raid. The letter shows his research network in action, with manuscripts and case files passed to a school contact in Atlanta. It also shows how widely his interests ranged beyond the Kennedy case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DavidovLeonard_: Notes written by Heman Ramsey on July 9, 1975 concern a man named Leonard Davidov. The surviving record identifies the note-taker, the subject, and the date, but it does not explain who Davidov was or why Ramsey was recording information about him. The notes survive as a dated research file, one researcher's working record on a single individual.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GallenRichard_G: Harold Weisberg wrote to Richard Gallen on March 12 about Dr. Hufnagle and the subject of ESP. A letter from the fact-bound assassination researcher touching extrasensory perception is an odd corner of his correspondence. The surviving record gives the date in short form, the two names, and the topic, but no text, so the entry stands as a dated Weisberg letter on an unlikely subject.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JFKHonorGuard_J: Volume 1, issue 3 of JFK Honor Guard, dated July 1992, is an issue of a newsletter named for the honor guard tied to President Kennedy's memory. The surviving record gives the title, volume, issue, and date but no contents or publisher detail. The entry stands as a dated 1992 issue of that newsletter, kept among the archive's assassination-era periodicals.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LeeBernard_Lee_:
A federal judge ordered the FBI to hand over its tapes and transcripts from the wiretapping of Martin Luther King Jr. Under the order, the material went to the National Archives, sealed for thirty years. The suit that forced the order was brought by Bernard Lee, a close King aide, and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

The FBI had recorded King for years, and what should happen to those recordings stayed in court long after his death. The order split the difference: the tapes were preserved, but locked away for a generation. The news report records the ruling, the archive named to hold the material, and the men and organization who won it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LubicRichard_Lu: Optical character recognition was run over the business card of Richard Lubic. The card names him as president of Color Corporation, a subsidiary of Gyro Dynamics Corporation. The address printed on it is 9000 Sunset Boulevard, Los Angeles. Business cards survive in research files because they fix a name, a job, and a place at a moment in time. This one records Lubic's role and where his company could be reached.
historic-doubts-on-the-life-and-reign-of:
Horace Walpole wrote this defence of Richard the Third, first issued at London in 1768. He calls blind trust in set characters a kind of literary superstition. Good or bad, he says, no fame should bar a fresh test. Richard's fame, fixed by his foes, was due for one.

Walpole weighs More and his copyists against hard records. He prizes a great wardrobe roll that runs from Edward the Fourth's death. Its keeper lists stuff, contracts, and costs for the coronation. From such dry facts Walpole builds doubt. Readers meet an early, sharp case for reading history against the grain.
in-the-days-of-poor-richard:
Irving Bacheller wrote In the Days of Poor Richard, a novel of the American founding, published in 1922. He dedicated it to Albert J. Beveridge as a student of the founders. Frontispiece art shows young John Irons and Margaret Hare in the forest. Chapters move from Horse Valley to Philadelphia and London.

Jack sees London and the great philosopher, Benjamin Franklin, in one part. Later parts put him in the service of the commander-in-chief and in Boston Jail. A woman called Little White Birch bids him farewell in a moving scene. Love and revolution run together.
jack-sheppard:
William Harrison Ainsworth, born at Manchester in 1805, made Jack Sheppard famous in 1839. This Penguin edition opens with his life, from solicitor's training to Rookwood in 1834. Rookwood popularized highwayman Dick Turpin, the life notes say. Ainsworth hosted Thackeray, Carlyle, and the young Dickens in London literary circles.

Jack Sheppard, the thief and prison breaker, rides the novel's center. Horsemen dash along the Edgware Road and turn toward Paddington Green in one chase scene. Jonathan Wild, the thief taker, hunts him through old London. The romance turned a real criminal into a popular hero.
jane-allen-right-guard:
Edith Bancroft wrote Jane Allen, Right Guard, a school story published in 1918. It follows her Jane Allen of the Sub-Team. Day dreams and a council of war open the book at Wellington. Bad news, an unknown mischief maker, and an unpleasant tablemate raise the stakes.

Tryouts for the team end in a spirited basket-ball exhibition in one scene. Ten girls play with strong determination to be among the elect, the text says. Breathless, they await the verdict off the floor. An accusation, a star witness, and reinstatement fill the later chapters. Jane's honor and game are both defended.
juvenal-satires-persius-gifford:
