Juvenal wrote sixteen fierce satires on Roman life around the early second century. Lewis Evans gave a literal prose version, and William Gifford added his famous verse rendering. Persius, Sulpicia, and fragments of Lucilius complete the volume.

Juvenal attacks corrupt nobles, greedy legacy hunters, and noisy city streets. His phrase about bread and circuses comes from these poems. Persius writes tighter, more Stoic satires on folly and freedom of mind. The Bohn Classical Library edition put both translators between one set of covers. Angry, funny, and often obscene, Roman satire here shows its full range and bite.
kilmeny-of-the-orchard:
Kilmeny of the Orchard is a novel by L. M. Montgomery, dedicated to her cousin Beatrice A. McIntyre. An epigraph from Hogg's Queen's Wake describes Kilmeny: still-faced, with a cheek like a moss rose. Her voice, the verse says, is like a distant melody. A verse from Kipling's The Light That Failed stands beside it.

Kilmeny is a Prince Edward Island girl who cannot speak, and her silence shapes the story. Eric Marshall, a young teacher, comes to her family's orchard world and learns her story. Montgomery, famed for Anne of Green Gables, gives this shorter novel the same island light. The epigraphs announce its mood: beauty, music unheard, and feelings words cannot carry.
looking-backward:
Edward Bellamy, an American writer, wrote this tale of a man who wakes in the year 2000, in 1888. Its full name adds the span 2000 to 1887, the year its hero falls asleep. The book sold in vast counts and set off a wave of clubs in its hero's name.

Julian West sleeps in a sealed room and wakes in a Boston made new and fair. Work, goods, and cash are shared by the state in a calm, planned scheme. The book gave the hope of a kind world a shape that men of its age could grasp.
lucretius-de-rerum-natura-leonard:
Lucretius, a Roman poet of the first century BC, wrote On the Nature of Things to free readers from fear. William Ellery Leonard's 1916 English translation renders the poem in strong blank verse. The poem teaches the system of Epicurus in six books of Latin verse.

Lucretius argues that all things are atoms and empty space, and that the gods take no part in human affairs. The soul, being atoms, ends at death, so death is nothing to fear. He treats the senses, the growth of human society, and the plague that struck Athens. The poem is both a physics and a cure for dread, and its science is startlingly modern in spirit.
lucy-raymond-or-the-children-s-watchword:
Lucy Raymond; Or, The Children's Watchword is a Canadian tale for the young. Agnes Maule Machar wrote it, as the author of Katie Johnstone's Cross. James Campbell and Son published it at Toronto. Chapters begin with Miss Preston's last Sunday and Lucy's home.

Nelly's Sunday evening, a strawberrying party, and a mission follow. Temptations, partings, and new experiences test the children. Lucy makes a start in life and learns what ambition costs. Friendship and faith guide her through each trial. The book belongs to the Sunday-school shelf of its day. It teaches kindness and trust in a gentle story form.
making-his-way-or-frank-courtney-s-strug:
Making His Way tells of Frank Courtney's struggle upward, by Horatio Alger, Jr. Whitman Publishing of Racine issued this boy's novel. Frank is a schoolboy when a telegram brings his bereavement. Mrs. Manning's will then leaves him disinherited and near penniless.

The Mannings' heir, Mark, yields to temptation and falls into trouble. Frank sets out for New York and seeks work in vain. A Wall Street adventure and a young tea merchant change his luck. He wins a place as a private secretary by honest merit. Alger's tale rewards pluck, temperance, and steady work. It is a classic sample of his rags-to-respectability stories.
martin-pippin-in-the-apple-orchard:
Eleanor Farjeon wrote Martin Pippin in the Apple Orchard as a prose fairy tale. J. D. Beresford wrote the foreword for American readers. He calls her gift rare, and ranks her with Stephens and de la Mare.

Beresford says five pages took him out of his tired work day. Sunlight, humor, and sweet surprise held him till the end. He wishes more readers the same joy, and trusts the tale to speak for itself from there. Beresford ranks the gift of true fairy tale above plain skill. He found that rare gift on show in her verse as well.
miracles-of-our-lord:
George MacDonald published these papers on the miracles of Jesus in 1870. He wrote them at request, he says, believing the miracles express Christ's unseen life. Since Christ came so that people may know God, MacDonald argues, every word and action of his matters. The chapters sort the miracles by kind.

MacDonald treats healings asked and unasked, miracles granted to friends' prayers, and the casting out of devils. Later chapters cover the raising of the dead, power over nature, and the Resurrection. He insists that believing in God makes the miracles no great extra strain. The book reads the Gospel wonders as theology in action.
nasa-tm-19690018395-a-comparison-of-thre:
Gerald E. Wilson, of Goddard's Laboratory for Theoretical Studies, compares three sets of higher order plasma equations. His paper, X-641-69-194, is dated May 1969, and he held a resident research associate post. Each set gives accurate approximate expressions for the average motion of a plasma. The plasma drifts in electric and magnetic fields that vary only slowly across it.

No inconsistencies are revealed by the comparison, Wilson shows. Two of the three techniques turn out to be completely equivalent. Most results of the third method can also be obtained from that equivalent pair. As a byproduct, the comparison yields a quantity that stays conserved along a particle's guiding center path. Chapters treat the Chew-Goldberger-Low theory and the guiding center plasma before the verdict.
nasa-tm-19710022798-piston-manometer-as-:
I Warshawsky of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an October 1971 vacuum congress in Boston. It presents a piston manometer as an absolute standard for checking vacuum gauges. At very low pressures, gauges disagree unless one trusted reference exists. Warshawsky's device measures pressure directly from force and area. No other gauge is needed to set it.

A thin round disc hangs in a hole in the chamber wall, nearly filling it. Gas flows through the narrow gap around the disc to a pump. A balance weighs the force the gas presses on the disc. Known weights calibrate the balance in place. The device covered the range from ten to five hundred microtorr with small error.
our-master-thoughts-for-salvationists-ab: General Bramwell Booth led the Salvation Army after his father William. He wrote Our Master as thoughts for Salvationists about their Lord. Its motto runs: as man He suffered, as God He taught. The hosted sample shows the title page and a contents list only. The chapters promise The Man for the Century, and The Birth of Jesus. Contrasts at Bethlehem and A Neglected Saviour also appear. No chapter of Booth's teaching appears in the sample.
oxford:
Andrew Lang, sometime fellow of Merton College, published his Oxford papers in a 1922 illustrated edition with color plates by George F. Carline. His preface disclaims any history of the university: these are merely records of the impressions made by this or that aspect of Oxford life as it has been in different ages.

Oxford, he writes, is not easy to design in black and white. On a wild winter day the sunshine fleets along the plain. Towers, floods, and trees gleam in watery light. Then the melancholy mist creeps back. The damp soaks into the heart of everything. Lang, novelist, folklorist, and classicist, writes of his own university as a lover sketches a face he knows too well to summarize.
peter-bell-the-third:
Percy Bysshe Shelley published Peter Bell the Third under the comic mask of Miching Mallecho, meaning mischief. The dedication, addressed to Thomas Moore under a playful name, introduces Peter Bell as the dullest of three Peter Bells. Wordsworth's Peter Bell poem had lately appeared, and Shelley's satire answers it.

Shelley's Peter changes colours like a chameleon and his coat like a snake: sublime, then dull, then prosy and dull, then ultra-legitimately dull. The poem follows him through respectability and religion into hell. It is Shelley's sharpest piece of literary mockery, aimed at a poet he thought had sold his gift.
polyaenus-stratagems-shepherd:
Polyaenus compiled his Stratagems of War in 162 CE for two Roman emperors. R. Shepherd's English translation appeared in 1793. The collection gathers some nine hundred stratagems from myth to Macedon.

Ambushes, feints, disguises, and mind games fill the eight books. Generals, kings, and even gods contribute their famous tricks. Polyaenus wrote for emperors marching to war against Parthia. He hoped past cleverness would inspire present victories on campaign. Shepherd's translation delivered the ancient handbook of battlefield cunning to English officers. Not every tale is true, and Polyaenus rarely cares. As a storehouse of military deception, the collection has no ancient rival. Kings, chiefs, and plain troops all get their due in its long lists of tricks.
prince-jan-st-bernard:
Forrestine C. Hooker wrote Prince Jan, St. Bernard, illustrated by Lynn Bogue Hunt and issued by Doubleday in a 1946 printing of her 1921 story. She dedicates the book to an American patriot, her father, Brigadier-General Charles L. Cooper, whose fifty-seven years of service ended at the last roll call in 1919. Her hero is a puppy of the Great St. Bernard Hospice, bred to the duty stated in the frontispiece caption: the duty of a St. Bernard is to save lives and be worthy of his ancestors.

Contents carry Jan from the hospice dogs and the land of snow to a new world and a land of no snow. California, where kindness fails and Jan learns to hate, lands in the pound, and must find his way back to his nature. Jan's trials teach the era's favorite lesson: breeding and duty will out.
quentin-durward:
Quentin Durward is a historical novel by Sir Walter Scott, set in the fifteenth century. In his introduction Scott describes an age when the feudal system was first openly abandoned for selfish ends. The spirit of chivalry that animated it, he adds, itself rested on generosity and self-denial.

Chief among the new men stands Louis XI of France. In Scott's portrait he is a king so purely selfish that he seems an incarnation of the devil. He is armed with a caustic wit. That wit mocks any act done for another's good. His cruelties, perjuries, and suspicions are made worse, Scott argues, by gross superstition, as when he made the Virgin Mary a countess and colonel of his guards.
songs-of-a-savoyard: Songs of a Savoyard draws its pieces from two books. One is the 1920 Macmillan edition of The Bab Ballads. The other is Fifty Bab Ballads of 1884. George Routledge and Sons printed that older book. The contents give page numbers for each song. The Darned Mounseer leads the list. The Englishman and The Disagreeable Man follow. Later songs name The Highly Respectable Gondolier. The Fairy Queen's Song and Is Life a Boon stand there. The Modern Major-General and The Policeman's Lot appear as well.
stepping-heavenward:
Stepping Heavenward, by Mrs. E. Prentiss, takes the form of a private journal kept by Katherine, who turns sixteen on January 15, 1831. Her birth date, January 15, 1815, stands in the family Bible in her father's hand, and she opens the journal with a string of firm new resolutions.

Katherine vows to please her mother more, to master her hasty temper, and to practice self-denial like the people in books. The first morning already tests her: she sleeps late, cannot find a clean collar, snaps at her mother at breakfast, and then hurries off to school. The journal form lets readers watch a girl measure her faith and conduct day by day, faults included.
the-adventures-of-gerard:
A. Conan Doyle wrote The Adventures of Gerard, tales of a Napoleonic cavalry officer, and his preface lays out the real memoirs from which the tales draw strength. Doyle hopes readers will trace the tales back to those springs.

He says the age was rich in soldier's matter, some of it the most human he has ever read. He names De Rocca's memoir of the war in Spain, told by a hussar, and De Naylies' account of the same war from a dragoon's view. A French quote at the front praises a brave man with a grain of folly in his bravery. Readers then meet Brigadier Gerard, vain, brave, and blind to his own folly, in comic war tales.
the-art-of-fencing-or-the-use-of-the-sma: Front matter opens a Dublin fencing manual of 1734, printed by James Hort at the sign of Mercury in Skinner-Row. Andrew Mahon, professor of the small sword in Dublin, turned the work into English from the French of the late Monsieur L'Abbat, master of the art at the Academy of Toulouse. A dedication to a lord follows, though a note warns that its first page is missing. Mahon declines to praise his lordship's family gifts or his father's high charge, and signs himself a most devoted and humble servant.
the-charm-of-oxford: J. Wells, M.A., Warden of Wadham College, wrote this portrait of Oxford, first published in 1920 and shown here in a revised second edition of 1921, with pictures by W. G. Blackall. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here, opening with Iffley Mill and a plate of Christ Church Cathedral from the garden. Two poems frame the book, one calling Oxford a home of lost causes and mother of movements, and one by Wordsworth on its spires. No chapter text follows.
the-crime-of-sylvestre-bonnard:
Anatole France's The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard opens with Part I, The Log, dated December 24, 1849. The diarist, an old bookman, settles into his study in a dressing-gown and slippers, wiping a tear the north wind over the quay drew from him. Ice crystals like fern leaves hide the Seine, its bridges, and the Louvre from his window.

His cat Hamilcar lies curled on a cushion before the fire, nose between paws. Bonnard hails him in grand style as a somnolent prince and night guardian who defends the old scholar's books from nibblers. The cat answers with a kettle-like throat sound, then lowers his ears at the mounting rhetoric. He plainly rates the housekeeper's talk, which always means a meal or a whipping, above his master's fine sounds.
the-devil-s-guard:
Talbot Mundy's The Devil's Guard, dated 1926, comes here as a Project Gutenberg of Australia ebook. Its contents list twenty-four chapters with full-sentence titles. They follow Chullunder Ghose, Benjamin, Painless Parker Ramsden, Jimgrim, Jeff Ramsden, and Narayan Singh. The path runs through the fanged jaws of the Zogi-la, a yellow lama, and spies, and a claimed manuscript in the handwriting of Jesus.

The opening prose turns reflective: we remark on the slowness of the snail and the tortoise, Mundy writes. But the processes of evolution are far slower, so slow they escape our notice altogether. None the less we are evolving, though fewer of us than we suppose. Supposition is the fumes of decomposing vanity, the tool by which the Devil's Guard beclouds the road we climb.
the-disguising-at-hertford: John Lydgate, whose dates are given as about 1370 to 1449, wrote The Disguising at Hertford, a verse play from about 1427. The pages present here are editorial notes for a text made with leave of the Master and Fellows of Trinity College, Cambridge, owners of the unique manuscript. The notes explain that the thorn has been rendered as th, stops added, and two gaps supplied from John Stow's sixteenth-century copy. They also treat the play's first performance at Hertford Castle, probably in 1427. The play's own lines do not appear here.
the-exploits-of-brigadier-gerard: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's The Exploits of Brigadier Gerard stands here in a printing that lists his whole shelf up front. Holmes books lead, from The Adventures to His Last Bow. Then come Sir Nigel, The White Company, and Rodney Stone. None of the tales themselves are shown. Only the author's book list is present. The hero named in the title is Gerard, a hussar of Napoleon's wars.
the-faithful-steward:
Rev. Sereno D. Clark wrote this prize essay on steady giving, The Faithful Steward, after a contest that drew one hundred and seventy-two entries. The judges split a prize of four hundred dollars among four works, and this is one of them.

Clark argues that giving by plan, not by whim, is a core part of Christian character. The book asks two hard questions: how much of a person's income should go to good causes, and on what rule that share is set. It then takes up how such a plan works in daily life, pressing readers to fix a share and keep to it.
the-golden-bird: Maria Thompson Daviess wrote The Golden Bird. The Century Company printed it in New York in 1918. Pictures are by Edward L. Chase. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a dedication, and a list of pictures. The picture captions show a girl called Polly kneeling before a sultan. They show a poor old sheep lying flat, with Adam over her. They show a baby in a feed basket, greeted by twin lambs. No chapter text is present.
the-house-by-the-church-yard: J. Sheridan Le Fanu wrote this novel. He was already known for Uncle Silas. The printing here is a Dublin edition of 1904. James Duffy and Company published it, with Macmillan in New York. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The chapter headings still sketch its world. A rector walks to his church at night. A coffin has no name. Royal Artillery officers give a dinner. Later headings mention a haunted house and a dead secret.
the-human-chord:
Algernon Blackwood published this novel in 1910. A three-word dedication fronts it: to those who hear. The first chapter returns to the hero's boyhood. His imagination was vivid beyond the usual. Everything he invented needed a real name. Nothing in his worlds lived until he found that name. The name was the breath of life.

One episode shows the gift's power and cost. He frightened his sister Teresa with an invented little man. The creature would pull out her hairs at night. The boy then sat guard beneath her window. He stayed from ten until four in the cold. He later claimed the creature, named Winky, had died. Blackwood builds a tale about sound and names. Spiritual forces become literal facts inside it.
the-late-miss-hollingford:
Rosa Mulholland, later Lady Gilbert, first placed her tale in All the Year Round many years before this reissue. Her preface says Charles Dickens chose the title himself and liked the story enough to ask her, then a young beginner, for a serial. French and Italian versions had already appeared abroad.

Chapter one frames the tale as an old lady telling on late autumn evenings. Harvest stores, honey jars, apples, and a sputtering parlour fire set the scene. A caption names Rachel returning to her mother, hinting at the family trouble inside the quiet frame.
the-law-and-the-word: T. Troward, a former divisional judge in Punjab, wrote on mental science and spiritual law in a book copyrighted in 1917. Only the title page and contents of the 1937 eighth printing are present here, listing chapters on facts in nature, psychic experiences, man place in the creative order, wholeness, and the promises. Troward argument linking spoken words to a universal law does not appear in this record beyond those chapter titles.
the-march-of-the-white-guard:
Gilbert Parker's The March of the White Guard opens at Fort Providence, a Hudson's Bay Company post, where chief factor Field turns from a frosty window. A letter in the monthly batch troubles him. It comes from the wife of a civil engineer of considerable fame who went to explore the Coppermine region and part of the Barren Grounds. He was due back in six months; a year has passed, and no word has reached any fort for nine months.

The Company backs the wife's plea for a relief party. Field objects that this is the arctic region, the task nearly hopeless, the fort small, and no men can be forced to volunteer for such a march. The question he puts to sub-factor Jaspar Hume hangs over the tale: who could lead such a party, and who could be found to follow?
the-phantom-herd: B. M. Bower, author of Chip of the Flying U, published The Phantom Herd in 1916. Front matter and a contents list are present, and no story text follows. Chapter titles mix ranch life with early motion pictures: The Indians Must Go, The Little Doctor Protests, A Bunch of One-Reelers from Bently Brown, and Villains All and Proud of It. A letter from Chief Big Turkey and a chapter on an Indian girl for a picture point the same way.
the-pleasures-of-england-lectures-given-: John Ruskin's The Pleasures of England collects lectures given in Oxford during his second tenure of the Slade Professorship. John Wiley and Sons published the edition shown at New York in 1888. It styles Ruskin honorary student of Christ Church and honorary fellow of Corpus Christi. Here only the title page, contents, and the heading of the first lecture appear, so the lecture text is absent. Four lectures are listed: The Pleasures of Learning, Faith, Deed, and Fancy. They run from Bertha and Alfred to Coeur de Lion and Elizabeth.
the-romance-of-a-christmas-card:
Kate Douglas Wiggin opens on Christmas Eve, a Saturday night, in Beulah, where Mrs. Larrabee leaves her minister husband revising his sermon to visit Letty, whose twins may be coming down with measles. She teases Luther that he looks like a blessed old prophet and asks his text.

The text proves to be Isaiah on being sent by the Lord, which Mrs. Larrabee says does not sound a bit like Christmas. Wiggin, who signs the copyright with her married name Riggs, sets up a holiday tale where duty and festivity pull gently apart. A card's romance will plainly start in this parsonage doorway talk.
the-thunder-bird: B. M. Bower's Thunder Bird was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1919 with a frontispiece by Anton Otto Fischer. This record holds the front matter and contents, ending at the heading of chapter one. Twenty-five chapters follow Johnny, who assumes a debt of honour, does stunts, finds fame, flies into Mexico and back, and takes the Thunder Bird up for a last flight. A frontispiece caption shows Schwab hanging back, unable to leave. Bower's flying Western is mapped here, though Johnny never leaves the ground in these pages.
the-visions-of-the-sleeping-bard: Ellis Wynne's Visions of the Sleeping Bard, in Welsh Gweledigaetheu y Bardd Cwsc, appears here in Robert Gwyneddon Davies's translation. Simpkin, Marshall published the edition in London in 1897, with the Welsh National Press at Carnarvon. A photograph shows Glasynys, Wynne's birthplace. Davies dedicates the translation to Professor John Rhys of Jesus College, Oxford, honouring his services to Celtic literature. The material present here stops at the head of the preface, so the visions themselves do not appear.
the-wizard:
H. Rider Haggard's volume gathers three tales, as his author's note explains. The Wizard tells of faith triumphing over danger in Africa. Elissa rebuilds the life of an ancient Phoenician city in Rhodesia. Black Heart and White Heart follows two Zulu lovers under King Cetshwayo. Haggard dedicates the book to a child, Nada Burnham, who died at Bulawayo in 1896.

Haggard admits that material for Elissa was scant. He adds a love story to suggest how the city fell. The tales mix adventure with questions of belief and loyalty. Courage is tested against war and custom. Readers of imperial-era adventure fiction will recognize Haggard's sweeping style.
the-young-guard: E. W. Hornung's The Young Guard, published in London in 1919, gathers wartime pieces that mostly appeared during the war. A contents list names poems such as Last Post and Wooden Crosses. The Ballad of Ensign Joy and Shell-Shock in Arras appear. The opening poem, Consecration, begins by addressing young soldiers as children. Only its first lines follow the contents in the pages present here.
through-space-to-mars-or-the-longest-jou:
Roy Rockwood's Through Space to Mars, fourth in the Great Marvel Series, opens in a laboratory with two chums, Jack Darrow and Mark Sampson. Jack asks for the large test tube and laughs about the last experiment, when a tube burst. Mark reminds him they both hid from the glass.

Jack measures a black chemical resembling gunpowder and fits a cork with a glass tube and rubber pipe. Mark begs for care while Jack teases him about ducking under the table. Readers get a boys' science adventure that begins with risky experiments and promises the longest journey on record.
tom-swift-and-his-sky-racer-or-the-quick: The Quickest Flight on Record names the goal in the Tom Swift sky racer story by Victor Appleton, laid out in twenty-five chapter headings. A prize offer opens the book, Mr. Swift falls ill, and the plans disappear. Tom builds the racer while Andy Foger prepares to contest the prize. The great race ends won by a length. Chapter one begins with a caller asking for Tom Swift, inventor of airships, then stops. The contents and that line are what is present here.
